summary: MPLS Network Actions are technologies that indicate actions affecting how a packet is forwarded or monitored along its label switched path, with any extra data needed. This informational RFC describes an architectural framework for MNA.

plainLanguage.summary: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) labels guide packets through a network. This framework describes how packets can also carry instructions for extra actions and the data those actions need.

subtitle: An architectural framework for carrying MPLS network actions and their supporting data.

tldr.problem: MPLS packets can carry labels for forwarding, but networks also need a shared framework for signaling additional packet actions and their data.
tldr.mechanism: A Network Action Sub-Stack groups a special indicator, action indicators, and optional data within or after an MPLS label stack.
tldr.outcome: This Informational framework has been updated by RFC 9994; it describes architecture and choices rather than one complete encoding.

facts.label: Action scopes
facts.value: Hop by Hop, Ingress to Egress, Select

today: RFC 9789 is an Informational framework and has been updated by RFC 9994. The RFC describes architecture and design choices; it does not itself select a complete encoding for all network actions.

sections.title: From Forwarding to Network Actions
sections.content:
MPLS forwarding actions tell routers to do extra work while forwarding a packet. The framework broadens this idea to network actions, including monitoring, security functions, and operations that are not directly about forwarding.

An action is triggered by an MNA packet, though it may affect later traffic. The framework is intended to support a shared set of actions and information elements for MPLS networks.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPLS packet can ask routers to do work beyond choosing its next hop. This framework describes how such requests can be carried in the packet.

sections.title: The Network Action Sub-Stack
sections.content:
A Network Action Sub-Stack (NAS) is a contiguous set of MPLS label stack entries that carries information about actions. Its first entry is the Network Action Sub-Stack Indicator, which contains a special-purpose label marking the start of the NAS.

The NAS may contain indicators that name actions and in-stack data that supports them. Some data may instead follow the label stack. A solution must define where sub-stacks occur, how data is encoded, and the order in which actions run.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS is a marked part of the MPLS label stack. It identifies requested actions and can carry the data they need.

sections.title: Scopes, Unknown Actions, and Readable Depth
sections.content:
An action may apply at every hop, only from ingress to egress, or at selected nodes. A solution that supports selected nodes must explain how it identifies them. A solution must also define what a router does when it sees an action it does not recognize.

Readable Label Depth (RLD) describes how many label stack entries a router can read without performance impact. A node that pushes a NAS is responsible for ensuring that nodes expected to process it can read the full sub-stack. RLD is advertised using IGP MSD-Type value 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Each action needs a rule saying which routers perform it. Routers also need enough readable label depth to reach the actions in a packet.

sections.title: Encoding and Defining Actions
sections.content:
The framework describes alternatives for identifying the MNA label, ending a NAS, and listing its actions. A solution may use a bit catalog or operation codes; each has different space costs depending on how many actions are present. The framework does not select one encoding.

A document defining an action must specify its name, indicator, scope, state effects, whether it is required, and the format of any in-stack or post-stack data. The framework calls for deterministic action ordering and recommends an IANA registry for actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Future specifications choose how to encode actions. Each action specification must explain its meaning, where it applies, and how to read its data.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
Network operators need to know which nodes support each action, and solution documents must describe management and diagnostic mechanisms. The MPLS forwarding plane has no built-in security mechanisms, so network operational security is important.

MNA data may be sensitive. The RFC describes a risk when one network carries another network's MPLS traffic by adding labels: MNA data from the inner network may be visible to capable forwarders in the outer network. It discusses rejecting untrusted MNA or fully encapsulating inbound packets as mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to track action support and protect sensitive MNA data. Extra encapsulation can keep another network's instructions from being processed unexpectedly.
